transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-04 09:32 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Tom (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Mike (Prospex CTO), Rosa (Prospex DevOps), Elena (Regulatory), Samir (Infra)
Shared artifacts: Redwood security pack (link), draft SOW template, Prospex rack spec (requested)

[00:00] Tom (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Tom, AE for Redwood inference. Today we're trying to understand Prospex's constraints for an on-prem airgapped deployment and how updates / patches would work given your regulatory needs.
[00:14] Mike (Prospex - CTO): Thanks Tom. Yeah, short background: we're a regulated genomics analytics firm, lots of patient data, so we need an airgapped private deployment. We're evaluating hosted/dedicated vs fully offline private. This call is to scope the latter.
[00:29] Rosa (Prospex - DevOps): Hi. Our biggest concerns are update cadence (we can't just pull images from the internet), hardware compatibility, and having cryptographically verifiable updates that our compliance team will accept.
[00:41] Priya (Redwood SE): Totally. We work with a couple of patterns: signed image bundles delivered via physical media, or an internally-run artifact proxy that you can sync from an isolated staging net. Either way we include signature verification and reproducible checksums.
[00:56] Samir (Infra): When you say signed image bundles, do you mean tarballs we mount and the runtime unpacks and verifies? Or some sort of signed container image? We run CentOS/Rocky on bare metal and a mix of BMC/IPMI-managed machines.
[01:12] Liam (Redwood SE): Good question. For Private we support a signed artifact format — we call it a release bundle — that includes a manifest, binary blobs, and a detached signature. The installer validates the signature against a Redwood public key; we can also integrate your KMS/HSM to do in-cluster verification.
[01:27] [small cross talk / inaudible]
[01:33] Dr. Elena (Regulatory): Important: any automated rollback needs to be auditable; we also need a test suite run on the update image and results archived for 7 years per policy.
[01:44] Priya (Redwood SE): We can integrate the update workflow with your existing CI test harness — we generate a reproducible test vector set (prompt/expected metrics) that runs during staging. We store test artifacts and signature metadata in the local audit store, which can be exported to your SEC/Reg team.
[02:01] Mike: For hardware, we have an existing GPU rack: initially two servers with A100 40GB each; we may add an H100 or AMD MI250 later. How does Redwood handle mixed-GPU fleets?
[02:15] Priya: The runtime supports heterogeneous backends. You can pin a model profile to a GPU type; we also can route by latency SLO or cost. Important caveat: quantization and kernel choices change per GPU, so identical behavior across A100 and H100 can vary slightly — we'll provide performance profiles for each setup.
[02:34] Rosa: What about NVMe caching and local disk? We need to know IOPS and sizing requirements for a given model size.
[02:42] Liam: For a 7B quantized model, expect ~40-80GB NVMe for model shards and an additional 10-30GB for KV cache depending on seq length. We'll produce a per-model sizing doc once you tell us model family and expected concurrency.
[02:58] Priya: Also note, for airgapped operation there's no remote artifact cache, so local caching is more critical. We recommend at least one fast NVMe per node and shared NFS only for logs/artifacts if you prefer.
[03:12] [00:03:12 timestamp noise]
[03:18] Samir: Patch windows — we currently have a quarterly security maintenance window and cannot accept rolling upgrades more frequently without sign-off. Can Redwood do single-shot upgrades that are fully reversible?
[03:29] Tom: Yes. Our canary/fallback logic is adjustable for Private. For airgapped installs the update process is manual-triggered by your ops with automated health checks. We can roll a new bundle to one node, run smoke tests, then proceed cluster-wide or roll back to the previous signed image.
[03:46] Elena: Who holds the signing key? Internal or Redwood? That matters for our auditors.
[03:51] Priya: We typically sign build artifacts on Redwood side for hosted flows. For customers requesting airgapped, we offer an option: Redwood-signed bundles plus an option to re-sign with your HSM before applying, or we provide unsigned bundles that you sign entirely in your environment. We can accommodate either with documented key custody flow.
[04:10] Mike: If we re-sign locally, how do we validate provenance of the build? We need chain-of-custody evidence.
[04:18] Priya: We provide a build manifest, reproducible hash list, and a signed CI artifact proving build provenance (timestamped). You can map that to your internal signing process.
[04:29] [04:29] Rosa: Network — we're truly isolated. No outbound. How do we handle telemetry, telemetry anonymization, and supportability?
[04:38] Tom: For Private airgapped we can ship a support bundle process: you generate a support snapshot locally (logs, traces, tokenized cost metrics without PII) and transmit out-of-band via SFTP or physical media to a Redwood secure intake endpoint. Telemetry is opt-in; nothing leaves without your explicit ops action.
[04:58] Samir: On the physical updates: do you have a suggested SOP for the USB/middleware method? We have strict chain-of-custody for physical media.
[05:07] Priya: Yes — recommended practice: use signed, checksummed release bundles on encrypted SSDs; the image includes a manifest with hash and signature; the ops person performing the upgrade logs BMC console output and signs the change record. We can provide a template checklist you can adapt.
[05:26] Dr. Elena: Would the audit logs include who applied what, when, and the signature fingerprint?
[05:33] Liam: Yes, audit log includes operator identity (SSO mapping or local user), timestamp, bundle fingerprint, and pre/post health metrics. Logs are persisted locally and can be exported to your long term archive.
[05:46] [05:46] Tom: Let's talk about model upkeep: you mentioned you might bring your own models vs using Redwood-hosted models. What is the plan?
[05:54] Mike: We have internal models (custom LLMs trained on de-identified clinical notes) and want to serve them on-prem. We'll want Redwood runtime to host those models but we cannot send training data to Redwood.
[06:06] Priya: Fine — the model files can be uploaded as part of the release bundle. We treat those as customer-owned artifacts, never uploaded to Redwood hosted storage unless customer explicitly opts in. We will provide model versioning and can assign model IDs only locally.
[06:18] Rosa: How are secrets managed? We use a hardware HSM for keys; we cannot have plaintext keys sitting on disk.
[06:25] Liam: Redwood Private supports external KMS/HSM integrations (PKCS#11, AWS CloudHSM, Azure KeyVault via VMs) or a local HSM through an adapter. Keys used to decrypt model artifacts can be wrapped and unwrapped inside your HSM; no unencrypted keys are stored long-term.
[06:40] [06:40] Mike: Latency expectations — for token-level latency we need sub-50ms 1-token tail for short prompts at 1-2 qps. Is that realistic on A100 40GB?
[06:53] Priya: Sub-50ms per-token tail is aggressive for certain model families; for a 7B quantized model we typically see mid-60s token latency on A100 depending on batch and KV cache hit. We can tune batching and prewarming to get closer, but there's a tradeoff with throughput. We'll provide a latency/throughput matrix in the perf profile.
[07:13] Rosa: Can we pin a model to dedicated GPU so it never moves? We want predictable latency.
[07:18] Priya: Yes — Redwood Dedicated style pinning is supported in Private: you can reserve GPUs to specific model groups. That gives predictable latency at the expense of utilization.
[07:27] [07:27] Samir: What about temperature / firmware concerns? We run 3rd party A100 blades and Son-of-Firmware updates are restricted. Do you require specific firmware levels?
[07:37] Liam: We have recommended firmware/driver versions per model kernel. We don't strictly enforce, but some performance/correctness paths rely on later drivers. For airgapped installs we can provide exact driver packages as part of the release bundle for you to install during maintenance windows.
[07:52] Dr. Elena: Any pre-certification or validation Redwood provides to speed our compliance sign-off?
[07:58] Tom: We can provide a validation checklist, sample audit evidence, and a template for your internal auditors outlining the update workflow, key custody, and rollback proofs. We also have customers that run a short validation run on staging hardware and Redwood runs the perf/quality checks remotely on a mirrored data set — but for full airgap you'll need internal validation.
[08:19] [08:19] Mike: On licensing and run costs — how is usage accounted in an on-prem pilot? Do we get metering?
[08:27] Tom: We include local metering that writes usage records (token counts, model IDs, inference counts) to the local metastore; you can export those to CSV for billing. For pilots we have a fixed pilot rate plus per-token for scaled production, negotiable in SOW.
[08:42] Rosa: Metering must not contain patient PII.
[08:45] Liam: Correct — metering strips PII; only numerical metrics are recorded.
[08:50] [08:50] Priya: Quick note on KV cache and prefix caching — because you have repeated prompt patterns in genomics pipelines, KV cache hits can massively reduce token compute. But caches are memory-sensitive; ensure you size the GPU memory for expected working set.
[09:06] Samir: For the pilot we're thinking 2 nodes, 2xA100 40GB each, 1 fast NVMe per node, and network isolated. Is that a reasonable starting point?
[09:16] Priya: That's a pragmatic pilot. We'll ask for expected QPS and prompt lengths to tune. For example at 3 concurrent users with avg 512 tokens sequence we can estimate throughput and provide a recommended next scale target.
[09:31] [09:31] Dr. Elena: Regarding retention: logs and audit trail retention — we need 7 years for certain artifacts. Will Redwood local store support that?
[09:39] Tom: Yes, logs are written to local long-term archive; retention is configurable. For very long retention we recommend exporting periodically to your long-term storage (S3-compatible in your airgapped case via offline transfer).
[09:52] Samir: If we do a physical transfer to Redwood for support, what's your data handling policy?
[09:58] Tom: We treat support bundles under strict controls: redacted PII by default, access controlled, retained only for immediate troubleshooting unless you explicitly request longer retention. We'll include that in the security pack.
[10:11] [10:11] Rosa: Can we get a whitepaper or playbook that shows the step-by-step for an airgap update including the commands and files involved?
[10:18] Priya: Yes. We'll attach a draft airgap playbook showing bundle format, verification commands, and checklist. That's one of the next steps.
[10:26] [pause / background]
[10:34] Mike: Slight pivot — what about model drift monitoring and quality regression detection? We need to ensure updates don't degrade outputs.
[10:42] Priya: Redwood Optimize has a quality monitoring pipeline that can run locally and compare metrics on a set of golden prompts. For airgapped installs we provide the evaluation harness to run inside your environment and produce a regression alert bundle you can review before accepting an update.
[10:58] Dr. Elena: Who sets the acceptance thresholds? Our compliance wants human sign-off for any model change affecting clinical interpretations.
[11:05] Liam: That's configurable. We can set automated prechecks but the final gating can be manual sign-off by your regulatory owner — the system will block rollout until you confirm.
[11:16] [11:16] Samir: Are there any known blockers for H100 / MI250 support in private? We're considering an H100 procurement next quarter.
[11:25] Priya: H100 is supported but some kernel paths and performance tuning differ; MI250 support exists for certain model types but overall it's less common so we may need a small validation pass. We recommend we run an initial perf/compat test on a single H100 node in our lab if you plan to adopt it.
[11:42] Tom: We can include that lab validation as an optional line item in the SOW.
[11:47] [11:47] Rosa: Last bit — incident response. If something goes wrong we need to know the on-call matrix and how Redwood will support us offline.
[11:56] Tom: For Private customers we provide a 24/7 enterprise support path with runbooks. For airgapped specifically we run remote consulting sessions via recorded BMC logs and optionally a ship-of-media escalation where we send a pre-signed recovery bundle on encrypted media.
[12:13] Dr. Elena: What's the expected lead time for us to get a pilot bundle and start a pilot?
[12:18] Tom: Once we have your hardware spec and sign-off on SOW, pilot provisioning typically takes 2-3 weeks (includes building the release bundle and validating it against your driver versions).
[12:29] [12:29] Mike: That timeline sounds okay. We'll try to get the hardware list over by next Tuesday.
[12:35] Priya: Great. We'll also prepare a short perf profile and a draft playbook.
[12:40] [wrap up]
[12:42] Tom: Recap — Redwood to send security pack and SOC/ISO extracts, draft airgap playbook, and pilot SOW. Prospex to send hardware list and compliance constraints doc. We'll reconvene after those artifacts to schedule an on-site intake.
[12:55] Dr. Elena: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:59] Tom: Thanks — we'll follow up in email and slack.
[13:04] [meeting end]

Notes about transcript quality: automatic transcription had occasional mislabels (e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache) and some overlapping talk in hardware discussion. Some company/product names may be slightly off in the ASR output.
